FACTORIZATION OF ELLIPTIC DIVISIBILITY SEQUENCES VIA MODULAR CURVES

BETÜL GEZER, İPEK ÇOLAK, OSMAN BİZİM Address: Uludag University, Faculty of Science, Department of Mathematics, Görükle, 16059, Bursa-TURKEY Email address: betulgezer@uludag.edu.tr, ipekk3353@gmail.com, obizim@uludag.edu.tr
Date: 06. 07. 2026.
Abstract.

In this paper, we give a structural factorization of elliptic divisibility sequences in terms of finitely many modular functions on the modular curve X1​(N)X_{1}(N). More precisely, we express the functions obtained by pulling back division polynomials along the universal torsion section as products of fixed modular factors. Then we show that this factorization is compatible with the natural action of (ℤ/N​ℤ)×(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times} on the modular curve X1​(N)X_{1}(N) and so descends to the modular curve X0​(N)X_{0}(N) via the norm map. As applications, we obtain a perfect power criterion, local and global growth estimates for the associated elliptic divisibility sequences.

Key words and phrases: 
Elliptic curves, division polynomials, elliptic divisibility sequences.

14H52, 11G05, 11G07, 11B37.

1. Introduction

Let EE be an elliptic curve defined over a field KK given by a Weierstrass equation

(1.1) E:y2+a1​x​y+a3​y=x3+a2​x2+a4​x+a6​, E:y^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{3}y=x^{3}+a_{2}x^{2}+a_{4}x+a_{6}\text{, }

let E⁡(K)E(K) denote the group of KK-rational points on EE, and let 𝒪\mathcal{O} denote the point at infinity, the identity element of the group E⁡(K)E(K). For background on elliptic curves, see [16, 17, 21]. The nn-division polynomial ψn\psi_{n} of EE is the unique function ψn\psi_{n} ∈K⁡(E)\in K(E) with divisor

div⁡(ψn)=[n]∗​(𝒪)−n2​(𝒪).\operatorname{div}(\psi_{n})=[n]^{\ast}(\mathcal{O})-n^{2}(\mathcal{O}).

Division polynomials play a central role in the theory of elliptic curves, e.g. they appear in height theory [17], in reduction theory [16], in algorithms for counting points on elliptic curves over finite fields [13], and in the theory of elliptic divisibility sequences (EDSs) [24]. See also [19], [1], [15].

The sequence of values (ψn​(P))n≥0(\psi_{n}(P))_{n\geq 0} of the division polynomials evaluated at a point PP satisfies the classical elliptic divisibility recurrence relations, see [24]. Hence, this gives rise to an elliptic divisibility sequence (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0~}associated to the pair (E,P)(E,P) where Wn=ψn​(P)W_{n}=\psi_{n}(P). The sequence (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0} is called the elliptic divisibility sequence associated to the pair (E,P)(E,P).

Pairs (E,P)(E,P) with prescribed torsion structure are parametrized by modular curves, providing a geometric way to study families of elliptic curves together with torsion points. This approach leads to a modular interpretation of elliptic divisibility sequences. Furthermore, we use the modular curves Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) and X1​(N)X_{1}(N) to analyze the sequences (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0}, where affine curve Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) parametrizes pairs (E,P)(E,P) with a point PP of order NN, and X1​(N)X_{1}(N) denotes its smooth projective compactification.

The aim of this paper is to interpret elliptic divisibility sequences (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0} associated to elliptic curves together with torsion points in terms of modular functions on Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N). The terms of an EDS can therefore be viewed as the specialization at (E,P)(E,P) of modular functions on Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N). Thus they are not merely quantities depending on a chosen Weierstrass equation, they arise from universal modular functions on Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N). We make this interpretation explicit and show that these functions admit finite modular factorizations with quadratic exponents depending only on nn modulo NN.

Furthermore, if we want these sequences to depend only on the elliptic curve over KK and the point PP ∈E⁡(K)\in E(K), but independent of the chosen model, we are naturally led to a canonical definition of elliptic divisibility sequences, obtained by pulling back the division polynomials ψn\psi_{n} along a section. More precisely, there exists a universal elliptic curve ℰ→\mathcal{E\rightarrow} Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) with universal section 𝒫\mathcal{P} :: Y1​(N)→Y_{1}(N)~\mathcal{\rightarrow} ℰ\mathcal{E}. Pulling back the nn-th division polynomial ψn\psi_{n} along the section 𝒫\mathcal{P} defines a modular function

(1.2) fn=𝒫∗​(ψn)∈K⁡(Y1​(N))f_{n}=\mathcal{P}^{\ast}(\psi_{n})\in K(Y_{1}(N))

where K​(Y1​(N))K(Y_{1}(N)) is the function field of the modular curve Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N), if n​𝒫=𝒪n\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{O}, then fnf_{n} vanishes identically. Now let Y1​(N)​(K)Y_{1}(N)(K) denote the KK-rational points on Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N), then for any (E,P)∈Y1​(N)​(K)(E,P)\in Y_{1}(N)(K), evaluating fnf_{n} at (E,P)(E,P) recovers the associated elliptic divisibility sequence, i.e.,

Wn=fn​(E,P).W_{n}=f_{n}(E,P).

Elliptic divisibility sequences over function fields have been studied by Ingram et al. [8] and others [2, 11, 12]. In the present work, we consider the functions fnf_{n} arising from the universal elliptic curve over Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) together with its universal section. This allows elliptic divisibility sequences to be interpreted in terms of modular functions and the geometry of modular curves.

In [6], elliptic divisibility sequences associated to elliptic curves over ℚ\mathbb{Q} were studied for specific torsion structures using explicit models of elliptic curves. By viewing these sequences as specializations of the functions fnf_{n} at points of Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N), we extend these results to elliptic curves over arbitrary number fields and to arbitrary levels NN. We further carry out these results on the modular curves X0​(N)X_{0}(N), which parametrize elliptic curves together with cyclic subgroups CC of order NN. Thus, we obtain a geometric interpretation of elliptic divisibility sequences both in terms of points and cyclic isogenies.

Our first main result gives a structural factorization of EDSs in terms of finitely many modular functions on X1​(N)X_{1}(N).

Theorem 1.1.

Let N≥2N\geq 2, let Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) be the affine modular curve parametrizing elliptic curves together with a point of order NN, and let X1​(N)X_{1}(N) be its smooth compactification with the function field K​(X1​(N))K(X_{1}(N)) over a number field KK. Suppose that (E,P)(E,P) correspond to a KK-rational point of Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N), and let (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0} be the elliptic divisibility sequence associated to (E,P)(E,P) via division polynomials ψn\psi_{n}. Then there exist finitely many modular functions g1,…,gr∈K​(X1​(N))×g_{1},\dots,g_{r}\in K(X_{1}(N))^{\times} depending only on NN and on the chosen model of X1​(N)X_{1}(N), such that

(1.3) Wn=∏i=1rgiαi​(n)(E,P) W_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}(E,P)\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ }

for all n≥1n\geq 1 such that N∤nN\nmid n, here each αi​(n)\alpha_{i}(n) is a polynomial in nn of degree at most 22 whose values depend only on the residue class of nn modulo NN, and each function gig_{i} has a divisor supported on the cusps and a finite set of points determined by the chosen model of X1​(N)X_{1}(N).

The proof relies on the existence of a universal elliptic curve ℰ\mathcal{E} →\mathcal{\rightarrow} Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) with a universal torsion section 𝒫\mathcal{P} of exact order NN. Pulling back the division polynomials ψn\psi_{n} along the section 𝒫\mathcal{P} we obtain functions on Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) and extend these functions to rational functions on X1​(N)X_{1}(N). Then we use divisor theory and evaluate these functions at (E,P)(E,P) to express WnW_{n} in terms of these modular functions.

We can extend Theorem 1.1 to the modular curves X0​(N)X_{0}(N), which parametrize elliptic curves together with cyclic subgroups CC of order NN. Since X0​(N)X_{0}(N) parametrizes cyclic subgroups without choice of generator, we choose a generator PP ∈\in CC to lift (E,C)(E,C) to a point of X1​(N)X_{1}(N); see [3, Section 1.5]. This lifting is well-defined up to the natural action of (ℤ/N​ℤ)×(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times}. Finally, by taking suitable products over all generators of CC, we obtain canonical functions on X0​(N)X_{0}(N). Then we show that the factorization structure descends to this setting.

The following theorem shows that the evaluation of the modular function fnf_{n} in (1.2) at a lifted point gives an elliptic divisibility sequence and that the factorization structure extends to this case.

Theorem 1.2.

With notation and assumptions as in Theorem 1.1, let fnf_{n} be as in (1.2). Let (E,C)(E,C) be a point of Y0​(N)​(K)Y_{0}(N)(K), where CC is a cyclic subgroup of order NN, and choose a generator P∈CP\in C, yielding a lift (E,P)∈Y1​(N)​(K)(E,P)\in Y_{1}(N)(K). Then the sequence

Wn=fn​(E,P)W_{n}=f_{n}(E,P)

is an elliptic divisibility sequence. Moreover, this sequence satisfies the factorization in (1.3).

Note that choosing a generator P∈CP\in C lifts (E,C)(E,C) to a point of Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N). This is compatible with the natural action of (ℤ/N​ℤ)×(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times} and so descends to X0​(N)X_{0}(N) via the norm map. The next theorem describes this descent in terms of modular functions.

Theorem 1.3.

With notation and assumptions as in Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, define

Fn=NmK⁡(X1​(N))/K⁡(X0​(N))​(fn)​,F_{n}=\mathrm{Nm}_{K(X_{1}(N))/K(X_{0}(N))}(f_{n})\text{,}

where NmK⁡(X1​(N))/K⁡(X0​(N))\mathrm{Nm}_{K(X_{1}(N))/K(X_{0}(N))} denotes norm for K⁡(X1​(N))/K⁡(X0​(N))K(X_{1}(N))/K(X_{0}(N)). Then the function FnF_{n} in K​(X0​(N))×K(X_{0}(N))^{\times} and for any (E,C)∈Y0​(N)​(K)(E,C)\in Y_{0}(N)(K) and any generator P∈CP\in C, we have

Fn​(E,C)=∏k∈(ℤ/N​ℤ)×fn​(E,k​P).F_{n}(E,C)=\prod_{k\in(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}f_{n}(E,kP).

Furthermore, the functions FnF_{n} satisfy the following factorization

Fn=∏i=1rGiαi​(n),F_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}G_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)},

where Gi=NmK⁡(X1​(N))/K⁡(X0​(N))​(gi)∈K​(X0​(N))×G_{i}=\mathrm{Nm}_{K(X_{1}(N))/K(X_{0}(N))}(g_{i})\in K(X_{0}(N))^{\times}.

2. Division Polynomials and Elliptic Divisibility Sequences

Recall that for an elliptic curve EE over a number field KK given by a Weierstrass equation (1.1) and a point P=(x,y)∈E⁡(K)P=(x,y)\in E(K), the division polynomials are defined using the initial values

together with the recursive relations

ψ2​n+1​(P)\displaystyle\psi_{2n+1}(P) =ψn+2​(P)​ψn​(P)3−ψn−1​(P)​ψn+1​(P)3​, for ​n≥2​,\displaystyle=\psi_{n+2}(P)\psi_{n}(P)^{3}-\psi_{n-1}(P)\psi_{n+1}(P)^{3}\text{, \ \ for }n\geq 2\text{,}

−ψn−2(P)ψn(P)ψn+1(P)3)(ψ2(P))−1, for n≥3.\displaystyle\ \ -\psi_{n-2}(P)\psi_{n}(P)\psi_{n+1}(P)^{3})(\psi_{2}(P))^{-1}\text{, \ \ for }n\geq 3\text{.}

where bib_{i}’s are usual quantities in [17, Chapter III]. In particular the sequence (ψn​(P))(\psi_{n}(P)) satisfies the recurrence relation (2.3).

An elliptic divisibility sequence (EDS) is a sequence (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0} satisfying a nonlinear recurrence

(2.3) Wm+n​Wm−n=Wm+1​Wm−1​Wn2−Wn+1​Wn−1​Wm2W_{m+n}W_{m-n}=W_{m+1}W_{m-1}W_{n~}^{2}-W_{n+1}W_{n-1}W_{m~}^{2}

and the divisibility property

Wn​|Wm​ whenever ​n|​mW_{n}|W_{m}\text{ whenever }n|m

for all m≥n≥1m\geq n\geq 1. See; [24], [25], [4], [14], and [23] for background on EDSs. An elliptic divisibility sequence is called proper if W0=0W_{0}=0, W1=1W_{1}=1, and W2​W3≠0W_{2}W_{3}\neq 0. A proper elliptic divisibility sequence is called nonsingular if its discriminant is non zero; see [19], [20] or [24] for the explicit formula of the discriminant of an EDS.

The arithmetic properties of these sequences were first studied by Ward [24, 25]. Ward [24, Theorem 12.1] showed that nonsingular elliptic divisibility sequences arise as values of the division polynomials of an elliptic curve. More precisely, he proved that if (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0} is a nonsingular elliptic divisibility sequence, then there exist a lattice L⊂ℂL\subset\mathbb{C} and a complex number zz ∈ℂ\in\mathbb{C} such that

Wn=ψn(z, L)=σ⁡(n​z​, ​L)σ(z, L)n2 for all n≥1,W_{n}=\psi_{n}(z\text{, }L)=\frac{\sigma(nz\text{, }L)}{\sigma(z\text{, }L)^{n^{2}}}\text{~\ \ for all }n\geq 1\text{,}

where ψn​(zCLOSE\psi_{n}(z, OPENL)L) and σ⁡(zCLOSE\sigma(z, OPENL)L) are the nn-division polynomial and the Weierstrass σ\sigma-function associated to the lattice LL, respectively. Subsequently, Silverman [19, Proposition 18] reformulated Ward’s result in an arithmetic setting over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, relating nonsingular elliptic divisibility sequences to division polynomials evaluated at rational points on elliptic curves. In the present paper, we work over an arbitrary number field KK. Thus for an elliptic curve EE over KK and a point P∈E⁡(K)P\in E(K), we use the normalization

(2.4) Wn=ψn​(P)​ for all ​n≥1W_{n}=\psi_{n}(P)\text{ \ \ \ for all }n\geq 1

where ψn\psi_{n} is the nn-division polynomial on EE. Furthermore, the sequence (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0} is the elliptic divisibility sequence associated to the pair (E,P)(E,P).

We now relate these arithmetic properties to the modular framework used throughout the paper. Let ℰ→\mathcal{E\rightarrow} Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) be the universal elliptic curve with universal section 𝒫\mathcal{P} :: Y1​(N)→Y_{1}(N)~\mathcal{\rightarrow} ℰ\mathcal{E}. Pulling back the nn-th division polynomial ψn\psi_{n} along 𝒫\mathcal{P} defines a modular function

(2.5) fn=𝒫∗​(ψn)∈K​(Y1​(N))×f_{n}=\mathcal{P}^{\ast}(\psi_{n})\in K(Y_{1}(N))^{\times}

where K​(Y1​(N))K(Y_{1}(N)) is the function field of the modular curve Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N), if n​𝒫=𝒪n\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{O}, then fnf_{n} vanishes identically. For a KK-rational point (E,P)∈Y1​(N)​(K)(E,P)\in Y_{1}(N)(K), evaluating fnf_{n} at (E,P)(E,P) gives

fn​(E,P)=ψn​(P)=Wn.f_{n}(E,P)=\psi_{n}(P)=W_{n}.

Thus by evaluating fnf_{n} at (E,P)(E,P), we recover the associated elliptic divisibility sequence.

3. Factorization and Applications

In this section, we show the factorization of the functions fn=𝒫∗​(ψn)f_{n}=\mathcal{P}^{\ast}(\psi_{n}) and obtain a perfect power criterion. Then we discuss the growth of the sequence (Wn)n≥0=(fn​(E,P))n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0}=(f_{n}(E,P))_{n\geq 0}. We illustrate the results with an explicit example in the case N=13N=13. Further examples for other levels, derived from the models presented in [22, pp. 1144-1145], which provide relatively simple factorization formulas for elliptic divisibility sequences, are given in the Appendix.

3.1. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Let ℰ→Y1​(N)\mathcal{E}\rightarrow Y_{1}(N) denote the universal elliptic curve with universal torsion section 𝒫\mathcal{P} of exact order NN. For each integer n≥1n\geq 1, we consider the nn-th division polynomial ψn\psi_{n} as a rational function on ℰ\mathcal{E} with divisor

div⁡(ψn)=∑𝒯∈ℰ⁡[n](𝒯)−n2​(𝒪)​.\operatorname{div}(\psi_{n})=\sum_{\mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{E}[n]}(\mathcal{T})-n^{2}(\mathcal{O})\text{.}

Pulling back ψn\psi_{n} via the universal section 𝒫\mathcal{P}, we obtain a rational function

fn=𝒫∗​(ψn)∈K​(Y1​(N))×f_{n}=\mathcal{P}^{\ast}(\psi_{n})\in K(Y_{1}(N))^{\times}

whose divisor is given by

div⁡(fn)=div⁡(𝒫∗​(ψn))=𝒫∗​(div⁡(ψn))=∑𝒯∈ℰ⁡[n]𝒫∗​(𝒯)−n2​𝒫∗​(𝒪)​.\operatorname{div}(f_{n})=\operatorname{div}(\mathcal{P}^{\ast}(\psi_{n}))=\mathcal{P}^{\ast}(\operatorname{div}(\psi_{n}))=\sum_{\mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{E}[n]}\mathcal{P}^{\ast}(\mathcal{T})-n^{2}\mathcal{P}^{\ast}(\mathcal{O})\text{.}

Since 𝒫\mathcal{P} has exact order NN, an equality 𝒫\mathcal{P} == 𝒯\mathcal{T} for some 𝒯∈ℰ⁡[n]\mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{E}[n] is possible if and only if N|nN~|~n. If N|nN~|~n, then fnf_{n} vanishes identically and its divisor is undefined. Thus we assume that N∤nN\nmid n. In this case, 𝒫\mathcal{P} never intersects the nn-torsion subgroup over Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N), thus fnf_{n} has no zeros or poles on this curve. Consequently, fnf_{n} is a modular unit, and the support of div⁡(fn)\operatorname{div}(f_{n}) is contained in the finite set of cusps of X1​(N)X_{1}(N). Moreover, the multiplicities in div⁡(ψn)\operatorname{div}(\psi_{n}) depend quadratically on nn. Pulling back along the section 𝒫\mathcal{P} preserves this growth. Therefore, the coefficients arising in the divisor decomposition of fnf_{n} at the cusps are polynomials in nn of degree at most 22. For certain residue classes modulo NN, ramification at the cusps may introduce cancellations that eliminate the quadratic term, reducing these coefficients to linear or constant polynomials.

Now passing to the smooth compactification X1​(N)X_{1}(N), the divisors appearing above are supported on a finite set of X1​(N)X_{1}(N) consisting of cusps and finitely many non-cuspidal points arising from the chosen model. The group of divisors supported on this finite set is finitely generated. Now we choose divisors D1,…,DrD_{1},\dots,D_{r} generating the subgroup of principal divisors div⁡(fn)\operatorname{div}(f_{n}). Then there exist polynomials αi​(n)\alpha_{i}(n) in nn of degree at most 22 taking integer values on suitable residue classes nn modulo NN, such that

div⁡(fn)=∑i=1rαi​(n)​Di.\operatorname{div}(f_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\alpha_{i}(n)D_{i}.

Since each DiD_{i} is principal, we can choose functions gi∈K​(X1​(N))×g_{i}\in K(X_{1}(N))^{\times} with div⁡(gi)=Di\operatorname{div}(g_{i})=D_{i}, where the divisors of these gig_{i} are supported on the cusps along with a finite set of non-cuspidal points arising from the coordinate singularities of the chosen model. Now define

Fn=∏i=1rgiαi​(n)​.F_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}\text{.}

Thus div⁡(Fn)=div⁡(fn)\operatorname{div}(F_{n})=\operatorname{div}(f_{n}), which implies div⁡(Fn/fn)=0\operatorname{div}(F_{n}/f_{n})=0. This means that Fn/fnF_{n}/f_{n} =cn=c_{n} for some cn∈K×c_{n}\in K^{\times}, yielding Fn=cn​fnF_{n}=c_{n}f_{n}. By identifying cn​fnc_{n}f_{n} with fnf_{n}, we finally obtain Fn=fnF_{n}=f_{n}. Then evaluating each fnf_{n} at a KK-rational point (E,P)(E,P) of Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N), we have

Wn=fn​(E,P)=∏i=1rgiαi​(n)​(E,P).W_{n}=f_{n}(E,P)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}(E,P).

∎

Remark 3.1.

The bound deg⁡(αi​(n))≤2\deg(\alpha_{i}(n))\leq 2 reflects the quadratic growth of the division polynomials on the universal elliptic curve. Geometrically, degree drops may be interpreted in terms of ramification behavior of the section 𝒫\mathcal{P} and special torsion relations among the points n​PnP (for an explicit example, see the case N=18N=18 in the Appendix, where α2​(n)=1,\alpha_{2}(n)=1, if nn ≡9​(18)\equiv 9~(18) or α2​(n)=0,\alpha_{2}(n)=0, otherwise). Thus, lower-degree exponents should be viewed as a natural feature of the geometry rather than an exception.

As an illustration of Theorem 1.1, we give an explicit factorization of the terms of the sequence for N=13N=13, see the Appendix for additional examples. admits the following factorization.

3.2. Perfect Power Structure

Theorem 1.1 gives a criterion for when the modular function fnf_{n} is an mm-th power in K​(X1​(N))K(X_{1}(N)). After evaluating at a point (E,P)∈Y1​(N)​(K)(E,P)\in Y_{1}(N)(K) yields perfect power terms in the associated elliptic divisibility sequence.

Theorem 3.2.

With notation and assumptions as in Theorem 1.1, let fn∈K⁡(X1​(N))f_{n}\in K(X_{1}(N)) be as in (1.2). Suppose that

div⁡(fn)=∑i=1rαi​(n)​Di,\operatorname{div}(f_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\alpha_{i}(n)\,D_{i},

where each DiD_{i} is a principal divisor on X1​(N)X_{1}(N), and Di=div⁡(gi)D_{i}=\operatorname{div}(g_{i}) for gi∈K​(X1​(N))×g_{i}\in K(X_{1}(N))^{\times}. If for some integer m≥2m\geq 2 one has αi​(n)∈m​ℤ\alpha_{i}(n)\in m\mathbb{Z} for all i=1,…,ri=1,...,r, then there exist hn∈K​(X1​(N))×h_{n}\in K(X_{1}(N))^{\times} and cn∈K×c_{n}\in K^{\times} such that fn=cn​hnmf_{n}=c_{n}h_{n}^{m}. In particular, if cn∈Kmc_{n}\in K^{m}, then fnf_{n} is an mm-th power in K​(X1​(N))×K(X_{1}(N))^{\times}.

Proof.

By the proof of Theorem 1.1, the function fnf_{n} can be written as a product of modular functions gig_{i} with polynomials αi​(n)\alpha_{i}(n) in nn of degree at most 22 for all i=1,…,ri=1,...,r. By assumption we can write αi​(n)=m​βi​(n)\alpha_{i}(n)=m\beta_{i}(n) for some integers βi​(n)\beta_{i}(n). Therefore

div⁡(fn)=∑i=1rm​βi​(n)​div⁡(gi).\operatorname{div}(f_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}m\beta_{i}(n)\operatorname{div}(g_{i}).

and so

div⁡(fn)=m​div⁡(∏i=1rgiβi​(n)).\operatorname{div}(f_{n})=m\operatorname{div}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\beta_{i}(n)}\right).

Now set

hn=∏i=1rgiβi​(n).h_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\beta_{i}(n)}.

Then div⁡(fn)=div⁡(hnm)\operatorname{div}(f_{n})=\operatorname{div}(h_{n}^{m}) and therefore div⁡(fn/hnm)=0\operatorname{div}\left(f_{n}/h_{n}^{m}\right)=0. Since X1​(N)X_{1}(N) is complete, every rational function on X1​(N)X_{1}(N) with trivial divisor is constant. Hence fn/hnm=cnf_{n}/h_{n}^{m}=c_{n} for some cn∈K×c_{n}\in K^{\times}. Therefore fn=cn​hnmf_{n}=c_{n}h_{n}^{m}. If cn∈Kmc_{n}\in K^{m}, say cn=dmc_{n}=d^{m} for some d∈K×d\in K^{\times}, then fn=(d​hn)mf_{n}=(dh_{n})^{m}. Hence fnf_{n} is an mm-th power in K​(X1​(N))×K(X_{1}(N))^{\times}. ∎

As an immediate result of Theorem 3.2 we have the following corollary.

Corollary 3.3.

With notation and assumptions as in Theorems 1.1 and 3.2. For every point (E,P)∈Y1​(N)​(K)(E,P)\in Y_{1}(N)(K) one has

Wn=fn​(E,P)=cn​hnm​(E,P).W_{n}=f_{n}(E,P)=c_{n}h_{n}^{m}(E,P).

Thus, if cn∈Kmc_{n}\in K^{m}, then WnW_{n} is an mm-th power in KK.

Proof.

Evaluating at a point (E,P)∈Y1​(N)​(K)(E,P)\in Y_{1}(N)(K) where all functions are defined gives

Wn=fn​(E,P)=cn​hnm​(E,P).W_{n}=f_{n}(E,P)=c_{n}h_{n}^{m}(E,P).

If cn=dmc_{n}=d^{m}, then

Wn=(d​hn​(E,P))m.W_{n}=(dh_{n}(E,P))^{m}.

Thus WnW_{n} is an mm-th power in KK. ∎

3.3. Local and Global Growth Estimates

The growth of elliptic divisibility sequences over number fields is classically related to height theory on elliptic curves. In the nontorsion case, logarithms of the values of division polynomials at a point are closely related to local and canonical heights; see, for example [5] and [18]. Since we work with torsion points, these nontorsion height estimates do not apply. Instead, the estimates below follow from Theorem 1.1.

The following theorem gives a local growth estimate for the sequence (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0}.

Theorem 3.4.

With notation and assumptions as in Theorems 1.1, let (E,P)∈Y1​(N)​(K)(E,P)\in Y_{1}(N)(K), let (Wn)n≥0(W_{n})_{n\geq 0} be the elliptic divisibility sequence over the number field KK associated to (E,P)(E,P) via division polynomials ψn\psi_{n}, and let υ\upsilon be a place of KK. Then there exists a constant Cv(E,P)>0C_{{}_{v}}(E,P)>0 such that

log⁡|Wn|υ≤Cυ​(E,P)​n2\log|W_{n}|_{\upsilon}\leq C_{\upsilon}(E,P)n^{2}

for all nn such that N∤nN\nmid n.

Proof.

By Theorem 1.1, we know that the modular factors gig_{i} are defined and nonzero at (E,P)(E,P), or equivalently, gi​(E,P)g_{i}(E,P) ∈K×\in K^{\times} for all ii and that

Wn=∏i=1rgiαi​(n)​(E,P)W_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}(E,P)

for all nn such that N∤nN\nmid n. Then |Wn|υ=∏i=1r|giαi​(n)​(E,P)|υ|W_{n}|_{\upsilon}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}|g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}(E,P)|_{\upsilon}. Since each gi​(E,P)g_{i}(E,P) ∈K×\in K^{\times} for all ii, taking logarithms we obtain

log⁡|Wn|υ=∑i=1rαi​(n)​log⁡|gi​(E,P)|υ≤∑i=1r|αi​(n)||log⁡|gi​(E,P)|υ|​.\log|W_{n}|_{\upsilon}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\alpha_{i}(n)\log|g_{i}(E,P)|_{\upsilon}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}|\alpha_{i}(n)||\log|g_{i}(E,P)|_{\upsilon}|\text{.}

Since each function αi​(n)\alpha_{i}(n) has degree at most 22 on residue classes modulo NN, there exists a constant Ci>0C_{i}>0 such that |αi​(n)|≤Ci​n2|\alpha_{i}(n)|\leq C_{i}n^{2} for all nn such that N∤nN\nmid n. Therefore

log⁡|Wn|υ≤n2​∑i=1rCi​|log|​gi​(E,P)|υ|≤Cυ​(E,P)​n2\log|W_{n}|_{\upsilon}\leq n^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{r}C_{i}\,|\log|g_{i}(E,P)|_{\upsilon}\,|\leq C_{\upsilon}(E,P)n^{2}

for some constant Cυ​(E,P)=max1≤i≤r⁡{Ci|log⁡|gi​(E,P)|υ|}>0C_{\upsilon}(E,P)=\max_{1\leq i\leq r}\{C_{i}|\log|g_{i}(E,P)|_{\upsilon}\,|\}>0. ∎

As another consequence of Theorem 1.1, we obtain a global norm estimate for the specialized EDS terms.

Corollary 3.5.

With notation and assumptions of the above theorem, define

En=|NmK/ℚ​(Wn)|E_{n}=\left|\mathrm{Nm}_{K/\mathbf{\mathbb{Q}}}(W_{n})\right|

for N∤nN\nmid n, where NmK/ℚ\mathrm{Nm}_{K/\mathbf{\mathbb{Q}}} denotes norm for K/ℚK/\mathbf{\mathbb{Q}}. Then there exists a constant C⁡(E,P)>0C(E,P)>0 such that

log⁡En≤C⁡(E,P)​n2\log E_{n}\leq C(E,P)n^{2}

By the proof of Theorem 1.1, for N∤nN\nmid n we have fn=∏i=1rgiαi​(n)f_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)} on each residue class modulo NN. Evaluating at (E,P)(E,P) gives Wn=∏i=1rgiαi​(n)​(E,P)W_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}(E,P). Taking the absolute norm for K/ℚK/\mathbf{\mathbb{Q}}, we obtain

En=|NmK/ℚ​(Wn)|=∏i=1r|NmK/ℚ​(gi​(E,P))|αi​(n).E_{n}=\left|\mathrm{Nm}_{K/\mathbf{\mathbb{Q}}}(W_{n})\right|=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\left|\mathrm{Nm}_{K/\mathbf{\mathbb{Q}}}(g_{i}(E,P))\right|^{\alpha_{i}(n)}.

Therefore

log⁡En=∑i=1rαi​(n)​log⁡|NmK/ℚ​(gi​(E,P))|≤∑i=1r|αi​(n)|​|log⁡|NmK/ℚ​(gi​(E,P))||.\log E_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\alpha_{i}(n)\log\left|\mathrm{Nm}_{K/\mathbf{\mathbb{Q}}}(g_{i}(E,P))\right|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}|\alpha_{i}(n)\,|\,|\log\left|\mathrm{Nm}_{K/\mathbf{\mathbb{Q}}}(g_{i}(E,P))\right|\,|.

Since each function αi​(n)\alpha_{i}(n) has degree at most 22 on residue classes modulo NN, there exists a constant Ci>0C_{i}>0 such that |αi​(n)|≤Ci​n2|\alpha_{i}(n)|\leq C_{i}n^{2} for all nn such that N∤nN\nmid n. Since the functions αi​(n)\alpha_{i}(n) have degree at most 22 on residue classes modulo NN, there is a constant C⁡(E,P)>0C(E,P)>0 such that

log⁡En≤C⁡(E,P)​n2.\log E_{n}\leq C(E,P)n^{2}.

∎

4. Lifting and Norm Descent

Let (E,C)(E,C) be a point of Y0​(N)​(K)Y_{0}(N)(K), where CC is a cyclic subgroup of order NN and choose a generator P∈CP\in C, yielding a lift (E,P)∈Y1​(N)​(K)(E,P)\in Y_{1}(N)(K) and let fnf_{n} be as in (1.2). In this section, we establish that evaluating the modular function fnf_{n} at this lifted point, i.e., Wn=fn​(E,P)W_{n}=f_{n}(E,P) defines an EDS. Furthermore we demonstrade that the resulting factorization structure descents to X0​(N)X_{0}(N) via the norm map.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Let (E,C)∈Y0​(N)​(K)(E,C)\in Y_{0}(N)(K) be given. Since CC is a cyclic subgroup of order NN, any generator P∈CP\in C determines a point (E,P)∈Y1​(N)​(K)(E,P)\in Y_{1}(N)(K), which is a lift of (E,C)(E,C) along the morphism

ϕ:Y1​(N)→Y0​(N)​, ​(E,P)↦(E,⟨P⟩)\phi:Y_{1}(N)\rightarrow Y_{0}(N)\text{, }(E,P)\mapsto(E,\langle P\rangle)

obtained by forgetting the generator, but keeping the group it generates; see [3, p.40]. By (1.2), the functions

fn=𝒫∗​(ψn)f_{n}=\mathcal{P}^{\ast}(\psi_{n})

are modular functions on Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N). Now evaluating at the lifted point (E,P)(E,P) gives

Wn=fn​(E,P)=ψn​(P),W_{n}=f_{n}(E,P)=\psi_{n}(P),

which is the elliptic divisibility sequence associated to (E,P)(E,P). By the proof of Theorem 1.1, the fnf_{n} can be factored as

fn=∏i=1rgiαi​(n)​,f_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}\text{,}

and evaluating this at (E,P)(E,P) gives

Wn=∏i=1rgiαi​(n)​(E,P)​,W_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}(E,P)\text{,}

where gi∈K​(X1​(N))×g_{i}\in K(X_{1}(N))^{\times} and each αi​(n)\alpha_{i}(n) is a polynomial in nn of degree at most 22 taking integer values on suitable residue classes nn modulo NN. Now let k​PkP be another generator of CC, with k∈(ℤ/N​ℤ)×k\in(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times}. Then (E,k​P)(E,kP) is the image of (E,P)(E,P) under the natural action of (ℤ/N​ℤ)×(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times} on Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N). Since this action permutes the factors in WnW_{n}, the factorization structure is preserved in the sense that the factors are transformed by the induced action while the exponent pattern remains unchanged. ∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.3.

Proof of theorem 1.3.

By the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, the functions fnf_{n} are defined on X1​(N)X_{1}(N) and their evaluation at (E,P)(E,P) is compatible with the natural action of (ℤ/N​ℤ)×(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times}, respectively. Since the morphism

ϕ:X1​(N)→X0​(N)\phi:X_{1}(N)\rightarrow X_{0}(N)

is a finite covering, the norm map

NmK⁡(X1​(N))/K⁡(X0​(N)):K​(X1​(N))×→K​(X0​(N))×\mathrm{Nm}_{K(X_{1}(N))/K(X_{0}(N))}:K(X_{1}(N))^{\times}\rightarrow K(X_{0}(N))^{\times}

is well-defined, thus Fn=NmK⁡(X1​(N))/K⁡(X0​(N))​(fn)∈K​(X0​(N))×F_{n}=\mathrm{Nm}_{K(X_{1}(N))/K(X_{0}(N))}(f_{n})\in K(X_{0}(N))^{\times}.

On the other hand, the function field extension K⁡(X1​(N))/K⁡(X0​(N))K(X_{1}(N))/K(X_{0}(N)) is a Galois extension with Galois group (ℤ/N​ℤ)×(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times}, where the group acting on sections via 𝒫↦k​𝒫\mathcal{P}\mapsto k\mathcal{P}, k∈(ℤ/N​ℤ)×k\in(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times}; see [3, Section 7.5.]. Hence, the function FnF_{n} is defined as the norm of the fnf_{n} over the group (ℤ/N​ℤ)×(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times}, which is given by the product of pull-backs along the sections k​𝒫k\mathcal{P} as

Fn=∏k∈(ℤ/N​ℤ)×(k​𝒫)∗​(ψn)​,F_{n}=\prod_{k\in(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}(k\mathcal{P)}^{\ast}(\psi_{n})\text{,}

(see; [9, Section 1.8], for more details). Evaluating at (E,C)(E,C) yields

Fn​(E,C)=∏k∈(ℤ/N​ℤ)×fn​(E,k​P).F_{n}(E,C)=\prod_{k\in(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}f_{n}(E,kP).

The independence of this factorization from the choice of generator PP follows from the proof of Theorem 1.2. Finally, applying the norm to the factorization given in the proof of Theorem 1.1,

fn=∏i=1rgiαi​(n)f_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}

and using multiplicativity, we obtain

Fn=∏i=1r(NmK⁡(X1​(N))/K⁡(X0​(N))​(gi))αi​(n)=∏i=1rGiαi​(n)​,F_{n}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(\mathrm{Nm}_{K(X_{1}(N))/K(X_{0}(N))}(g_{i}))^{\alpha_{i}(n)}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}G_{i}^{\alpha_{i}(n)}\text{,}

where Gi=NmK⁡(X1​(N))/K⁡(X0​(N))​(gi)G_{i}=\mathrm{Nm}_{K(X_{1}(N))/K(X_{0}(N))}(g_{i}). ∎

5. Appendix

In this appendix, we give the explicit factorization formulas over a number field KK for the levels N∈{11,13,14,15,16,18}N\in\{11,13,14,15,16,18\}. These cases are naturally motivated by the arithmetic of torsion points over quadratic fields. On the other hand, the levels NN ∈{2,3,…,9,10,12}\in\{2,3,...,9,10,12\} were studied in earlier works over ℚ\mathbb{Q} in [6, 7] and remain valid over any number field by base change. The additional levels treated here correspond to the quadratic torsion classification of Kenku and Momose [10]. We give only the formulas for the elliptic divisibility sequences associated to modular curves Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) in this appendix. A detailed proof is given in Section 3 for the case N=13N=13. The remaning levels can be proved in the same way, by using the induction and elliptic divisibility sequence recurrence (2.3).

For the remainder of the paper, we fix the models for Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N) given in [22, p. 1144] with coordinates (u,v)(u,v). Et:y2+(1−c)​x​y−b​y=x3−b​x2E_{t}:y^{2}+(1-c)xy-by=x^{3}-bx^{2}

with

c=s⁡(r−1),b=c​rc=s(r-1),b=cr

where Pt=(0,0)P_{t}=(0,0) is a point of exact order NN, and rr and ss are given functions of uu and vv; see [22, pp. 1144-1145], for models and birational maps. Evaluating the functions fnf_{n} at tt recovers the associated elliptic divisibility sequence

Wn​(t)=Wn​(u,v)=fn​(Et,Pt)​.W_{n}(t)=W_{n}(u,v)=f_{n}(E_{t},P_{t})\text{.}

We then express the functions fnf_{n} explicitly in terms of modular coordinates on Y1​(N)Y_{1}(N).
